function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish the task.  
I’ve also included the exact file contents that should be added to the repository.

> **⚠️ Important** – I can’t actually clone, commit or push for you, but the commands below will do it on your machine.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH access set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & create the required artefacts

> The repo is a very small Node.js “Hello World” app.  
> It contains:
> * `package.json` – lists dependencies (`express`, etc.)  
> * `app.js` – the entry point (listens on `process.env.PORT || 3000`)  
> * `README.md` – basic documentation

### 2.1 Dockerfile

Create a `Dockerfile` in the repo root:

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM node:18-alpine

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install app dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Bundle app source
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "app.js"]
```

> **Why this image?**  
> * `node:18-alpine` is lightweight and contains the Node runtime.  
> * `npm ci` guarantees a reproducible install from `package-lock.json`.  
> * The app listens on port **3000** – that’s what we expose.

### 2.2 Kubernetes YAMLs

Create a `k8s/` directory and add two files:

#### `k8s/deployment.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-deployment
spec:
  replicas: 2
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest   # <-- update with your registry/tag
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
        env:
        - name: PORT
          value: "3000"
```

#### `k8s/service.yaml`

```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome-service
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 80          # Service port
    targetPort: 3000  # Container port
```

> **What this does**  
> * Two replicas for high‑availability.  
> * Service exposes the app on port 80 inside the cluster (you can change to `NodePort` or `LoadBalancer` if you need external access).

### 2.3 GitHub Actions workflow

Create `.github/workflows/docker-build.yml`:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          tags: zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **Prerequisites**  
> * Create two GitHub secrets in the repo settings:  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
>   * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (or password)  
> * The workflow will run on every push to `main`, build the image, and push it to Docker Hub.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to Git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s/ deployment.yaml service.yaml .github/workflows/docker-build.yml
```

> If you want to keep the repo tidy, you can also add a `.dockerignore`:

```bash
echo -e "node_modules\n.git\n.gitignore\nDockerfile\nk8s\n.github" > .dockerignore
git add .dockerignore
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

Once the push lands, GitHub Actions will automatically start the build pipeline.

---

### Quick sanity check

```bash
# Build locally to make sure everything works
docker build -t zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest .

# Run the container
docker run -p 3000:3000 zelarhq/nodejs-welcome:latest
# Visit http://localhost:3000 in your browser – you should see the app’s response.
```

If the container starts without errors, your Dockerfile is good to go.  
If you deploy to a cluster, apply the manifests:

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s/
```

That’s it! 🎉

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tags, or service type to match your production needs.
